paras: The lynching near Comanche, Texas, was the killing in September 1882 of an unnamed Black man accused of raping a white girl, whom a posse pursued for ten miles, captured and lynched. The episode is known only from one-sentence telegraphic briefs that ran in papers from Tennessee to Dakota over the following two weeks.

According to a dispatch datelined Dallas, September 11, the man was accused of raping a white girl near Comanche on Friday, September 8. The same dispatch said that "a posse followed him ten miles, captured and lynched him", without naming the pursuers or saying how many there were. The reports do not name the man or the girl, and they do not describe how he was killed or where.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response to the lynching appears in the coverage.

The St. Paul Daily Globe carried the item first, on September 10, in its "Gist of the News" column, saying that "a negro, at Dallas, Tex., raped a white girl on Friday" and was followed, captured and lynched. A day later the same column ran a second, shorter version stating that the man was lynched "yesterday afternoon near Comanche" for "outraging a white girl". The Memphis Daily Appeal printed the fuller Dallas dispatch on September 12 among items grouped under "Rapes and Murders", and the Stark County Democrat in Ohio and the Mineral Point Tribune in Wisconsin reprinted it in their weekly digests.

Weeklies as far off as Romney, West Virginia, Miller, Dakota, and Grayling, Michigan, ran the short form in news-of-the-day columns between September 15 and 21. Every version stated the alleged rape as fact, identified the man only as "a negro", and gave the lynching without comment. No Texas paper's account was found, and the Black-press collection does not reach back to 1882.

The first St. Paul brief placed the assault "at Dallas", while the Dallas-datelined dispatch and later briefs placed it near Comanche, which suggests the Dallas dateline was read as the location. Reports also differ on dates: the Stark County Democrat put the alleged rape on Saturday rather than Friday, and the lynching was dated to September 9 by the South Branch Intelligencer but to the afternoon of September 10 by the Daily Globe. Because the Daily Globe had already reported the lynching in its September 10 issue, the September 9 date fits the earliest coverage better.

reader.title: Lynching near Comanche, Texas (September 1882)
bases: Every report says an unnamed Black man accused of raping a white girl was 'lynched', and the Dallas dispatch says a posse pursued, captured and lynched him (A9, A10, A7).

The papers say the man was 'lynched' by a 'posse' that captured him after a ten-mile pursuit over an alleged rape of a white girl (A9, A10, A7); no number of pursuers, method of killing or legal process is given, so the group's size is not stated.

All seven distinct reports are short telegraphic briefs that trace to wire copy out of Dallas (A5, A7, A9, A10, A11, A12); no local Texas account, named witness or independent investigation was found, though the briefs agree on the core event.

accounts.label: Short news-summary brief
accounts.gist: A Black man was lynched near Comanche, dated to the afternoon of September 10 in one version and to September 9 in another, for outraging a white girl.

framing.detail: Summary columns such as the Daily Globe's 'Gist of the News' and the Hand County Press's 'Briefs' ran a single sentence stating that 'a negro' raped a white girl and was lynched, with no comment.
The Memphis Daily Appeal ran the Dallas dispatch under a deck reading 'Rapes and Murders', and the Mineral Point Tribune under 'Criminal'.

conflicts.note: The Dallas version shares the Friday date and ten-mile pursuit of the Dallas-datelined dispatch that places the assault near Comanche, so Dallas is most likely the dateline, not the site.
The earliest prints, including the St. Paul brief of September 10, say Friday.
The St. Paul Globe was already reporting the lynching in its September 10 morning issue (A5), which fits September 9 better than September 10.
